summary: Defines the IBM Extended BCD Interchange Code (EBCDIC) and its mapping to ASCII so that every ARPANET host translates between the two in the same way. It describes the 8-bit EBCDIC character set and the extra characters needed.

plainLanguage.summary: Two computers use different alphabets, so this note is a translation chart. Everyone follows the same chart so letters stay the same.

questions: how is ebcdic mapped to ascii
why did the arpanet define an ebcdic mapping
subtitle: A standard way to convert between IBM's EBCDIC and ASCII text codes.

tldr.problem: Different computer systems use different character codes (EBCDIC for IBM systems, ASCII for most others), causing translation errors when they communicate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies three different correspondence schemes for mapping the 94 ASCII graphic characters to their equivalents in EBCDIC, plus mappings for control codes.
tldr.outcome: ARPANET sites that need to convert between EBCDIC and ASCII can follow the same standard mapping to ensure consistency.

today: The status of this RFC is unknown. It represents an attempt to standardize EBCDIC-to-ASCII conversion for early ARPANET communication, but the approach of soliciting community feedback without a clear resolution is not typical of later RFC standards.

sections.title: The Character Code Problem
sections.content:
EBCDIC is IBM's Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code, an 8-bit character set used by IBM computers. ASCII is the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, a 7-bit code used by most other systems. When an ARPANET host needs to communicate with an IBM system or translate files between them, it must convert between these two codes.

The problem is that the same byte value can mean different characters in EBCDIC and ASCII. Without a standard rule for translation, different sites would translate the same text differently, breaking communication.
sections.plainLanguage: When computers use different alphabets, the same letter looks different in each code. Everyone must agree on how to translate between them or messages get scrambled.

sections.title: EBCDIC Character Sets
sections.content:
EBCDIC defines 54 control codes (including space) and 88 graphic characters. The set includes a special graphics extension with 10 additional graphics borrowed from the 7-bit Hollerith code, and a publishing and printing option with 52 more graphics.

The RFC organizes EBCDIC codes into categories: CC (Communication Control), DC (Device Control), IS (Information Separator), FB (Format Bisector), ED (Edit and Mark), GH (Graphic Control), and CU (Customer Use). The RFC includes detailed listings of all control codes and graphic characters with their hexadecimal codes.
sections.plainLanguage: EBCDIC has a big table of codes for all letters, numbers, punctuation, and special commands. Different codes do different jobs like controlling printers or organizing data.

sections.title: Three Mapping Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC proposes three ways to map ASCII graphics to EBCDIC equivalents. The IBM Correspondence follows IBM's own recommendations, using special EBCDIC graphics for ASCII characters that have no obvious EBCDIC match. The Publishing Correspondence prefers characters from the publishing and printing option set because they appear on IBM TN print chains. The Graphical Correspondence chooses EBCDIC characters based on visual similarity to their ASCII counterparts, even when that produces unusual pairings like mapping ASCII reverse slash to the EBCDIC cent sign.

For the 34 ASCII control codes, the RFC specifies a one-to-one mapping to EBCDIC controls. For TELNET services over EBCDIC connections, it also proposes specific codes for sync, break, NOP, echo, and mode switching.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three different ways to translate: use IBM's choice, use characters that print well, or use characters that look similar. The RFC asks which way is best.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: This RFC is an ARPANET technical note from 1971 soliciting feedback from sites using EBCDIC. The document includes a questionnaire asking which correspondence scheme each site prefers and how their operating system handles the EBCDIC and control codes. It was intended to reach consensus on a standard EBCDIC-to-ASCII mapping for network communication.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1971, the RFC asked computer sites which translation method they liked best so everyone could agree on one standard.

references.text: Winett, J.M., "The EBCDIC Codes and Their Mapping to ASCII", RFC 183, July 1971.
